primary_claim: Most reported prompt-injection vulnerabilities against AI-assisted GitHub Actions workflows are not viable in practice because they rely on unrealistic access or overly permissive credentials or were never live-exploited, while GitInject, a framework that provisions real ephemeral repositories and triggers actual workflow runs instead of simulating them, discovered at least one real vulnerability (via actions/checkout's GITHUB_TOKEN storage) that was only discoverable through live execution since simpler attack attempts failed against sandbox and network constraints a simulator would not have enforced.
contradicts_or_qualifies: argues most reported prompt-injection vulnerabilities against AI-assisted GitHub Actions (e.g. PromptPwnd, a cross-repo leak that relied on an overly permissive organization-wide credential, and Wang et al.'s static-taint-analysis-derived vulnerabilities) are not viable in practice because they rely on unrealistic access, permissions, or were never live-exploited

shows a confirmed real vulnerability was only discoverable through real execution, since two simpler attack attempts failed against sandbox and network constraints that static analysis or a simulator would not have enforced
quote: Most of the reported attacks are proofs of concept that do not work in practice.
